solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old AEH sharp, sir? Possibly in his major work!

indicators.note: the question mark and 'Possibly' suggest these letters might be rearranged into something else

parts.note: taken as written; AEH are the initials of the poet A. E. Housman

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the old poet AEH was sharp, perhaps as shown in his greatest book.
explanation.walkthrough: AEH is A. E. Housman, whose best-known collection is the answer; Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border. 'Possibly' rearranges all of OLD AEH SHARP SIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Housman's 1896 cycle of poems is the masterpiece he is remembered for, so it is his major work.

clue.text: Being helpful type can be awful strain, a mum admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so one piece goes inside the other
something awful is in a bad state, so the letters of strain are jumbled

parts.note: mum and ma both mean mother

explanation.surface: A helpful person may suffer terrible stress, as a mother confesses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' belongs to the definition: a helpful being, not the verb it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Good Samaritan parable, the word names any kind being who helps a stranger in need.

clue.text: More than one spoke

parts.note: spoke looks like the past tense of speak, but it is a wheel's rod, and its plural in geometry is the lines from a circle's centre to its rim

explanation.surface: It seems to describe several people having said something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoke' tempts as the verb; it is the noun, a wheel's spoke being geometrically a line from centre to rim.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines from a circle's centre to its edge are what wheel spokes physically are, so the plural fits several spokes.

clue.text: Bird in region going over top of hill?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the next one

parts.note: a part is a region or area
a ridge is the long top of a hill, the question mark admitting the looseness

explanation.surface: A bird in some district flies over the brow of a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: A plump game bird of fields and hedgerows, shot for sport and food.

clue.text: Organic stuff brings nasty smell to you and me

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
you and me together are us

explanation.surface: Compost or similar matter gives off a stink that reaches us.
explanation.walkthrough: HUM is everyday British slang for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the dark organic material formed in soil from decaying plant and animal matter.

clue.text: Bouncy son, one to be found stuck in opening

indicators.note: stuck in means placed inside, so these pieces go within the opening

parts.note: a rent is a tear or split, an opening in cloth
I is the Roman numeral one
to lie is to be found or situated somewhere

explanation.surface: A lively boy and somebody else are trapped in a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be found' means to be situated, as in 'the town lies by the river'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something springy recovers its shape after pressure, which is what bouncy describes.

clue.text: Actress delivering short line, then short number

parts.note: L is a short form of line

indicators.note: short means cut, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: eight is a number

explanation.surface: An actress gives a clipped line of dialogue followed by a brief song.
explanation.walkthrough: Vivien Leigh, star of Gone with the Wind. 'short' removes the last letter of EIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Vivien Leigh was the English film star who played Scarlett O'Hara, so she is an actress.

clue.text: Presented article penned by two men

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Don and Ted are two men's names
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A piece of writing by two co-authors has been put forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something as a gift is to give it freely, the sense of donated.

clue.text: Grandma has place set up in French city

parts.note: nan is a familiar name for a grandmother

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means raised, so the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: to place something is to set it

explanation.surface: A grandmother has her home established in a city in France.
explanation.definitionFit: A port on the Loire in western France, it is a major city of the country.

clue.text: Trained ace, this writer's one who manages the paper?

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
this writer is the setter, me, and 'this writer's' is I'm, I am
an editor runs a newspaper, abbreviated ED

explanation.surface: A practised expert, the setter, claims to be the newspaper's boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Trained as in a gun or camera trained on a target, that is pointed at it.

clue.text: Let-up in respect of assigned task

parts.note: re means concerning, in respect of
a mission is a task someone is assigned

explanation.surface: A break is needed regarding the job handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: A period when an illness or pain eases is a let-up in its severity.

clue.text: English bishop gets into row, the dog!

indicators.note: gets into means goes inside, so these pieces go within the row

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: An English bishop squeezes into a line of seats with his dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed type of small, feisty dog originally used to hunt burrowing animals.

clue.text: Loony has kilt as formal item of attire

indicators.note: loony means crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A madman wears a kilt as his formal outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall glossy top hat is headwear worn with formal morning or evening dress.

clue.text: Have a meal, imbibing drink — and don't slouch!

indicators.note: imbibing means taking in, so the drink goes inside

parts.note: to sup is to eat supper
it is gin and Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: An instruction at dinner: eat, take a drink, and mind your posture.
explanation.walkthrough: IT is an old abbreviation for Italian vermouth, as in 'gin and it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to straighten their back in a chair is the opposite of letting them slouch.

clue.text: Sum up place with a cathedral to a T

parts.note: to precis is to summarise
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Summarise a cathedral town exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is a small English cathedral city near Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something to a T means doing it exactly, without error.

clue.text: Went down and ironed?

definitions.meaning: fell or became smaller in number
read as ..., with the creases taken out of a garment

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the jokey second reading: taking the creases out of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings: diminished in amount, and having had its wrinkles pressed away.

clue.text: Twister — such may set sail from Irish port

definitions.meaning: a spiral tool that twists into a bottle stopper

definitions.text: such may set sail from Irish port
definitions.meaning: read as ..., sailors from the Irish port of Cork

explanation.surface: A tornado might carry off sailors leaving an Irish harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Cork is a port city in southern Ireland; split the answer as CORK'S CREW.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiral-bladed opener twists into a cork, and the split phrase names a ship's company from that port.

clue.text: Easter run organised? I'm not hurrying!

indicators.note: organised means arranged, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A runner in an Easter race refuses to rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run' looks like part of the race; it is only fodder for 'organised'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroller is someone walking at a leisurely pace, so they could say this about themselves.

clue.text: Boy never poetic embracing French and becoming a poet

parts.note: a son is a boy

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the French word goes within

parts.note: ne'er is the poetic form of never
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A boy who is never lyrical takes up French and turns into a versifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of fourteen-line poems is a poet, the word sometimes used slightingly.

clue.text: Elevated status of smart drunk seen outside party

indicators.note: seen outside means surrounding, so the party goes within
drunk means reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: A smartly dressed drunk is spotted outside a party, a sign of fame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges the letters of smart into STARM before the party goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity status, being a star, is a raised standing in public life.

clue.text: Belief supported in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so the word is given by its sound

parts.note: trussed means supported by a truss or bound up

explanation.surface: A conviction backed up when it is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Faith or confidence in someone is a belief in their reliability.

clue.text: Emperor or Indian ruler invading borders of terrain

indicators.note: invading means entering, so the ruler goes inside
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a raja is an Indian prince or ruler

explanation.surface: An emperor or a maharaja marches over the edges of some land.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman ruler of the early second century, under whom the empire was at its largest.

clue.text: Bring action against revolutionary soldier invading Scottish isle

indicators.note: invading means entering, so the soldier goes inside the isle

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the soldier is read backwards

parts.note: GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A rebel fighter lands on an island off Scotland to attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge someone formally before a court is to bring a legal action against them.

clue.text: Unfortunate dears brought low

indicators.note: unfortunate means ill-starred, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Poor darlings humbled by misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a variant spelling of razed.
explanation.definitionFit: A building razed is levelled to the ground, literally brought low.

clue.text: Hundred up, a hundred — Hampshire's opener getting score!

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from the bottom

parts.note: a ton is a hundred
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: the opener is the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: a century is up, as Hampshire's opening batsman makes runs.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton and a century are cricket terms for a hundred runs; Hampshire is an English county side.
explanation.definitionFit: To score a mark is to cut a small notch, and to notch up points is to score them.

clue.text: Island having problem, a journey finishing halfway through

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

indicators.note: the word stops halfway, so its second half is dropped

parts.note: travel is a journey

explanation.surface: An island trip runs into trouble and ends early.
explanation.definitionFit: A large island of Indonesia, west of Borneo.

clue.text: Power of the ideal man taking out Rolls-Royce

indicators.note: taking out means removing these letters

parts.note: Mr Right is the ideal man to marry

explanation.surface: The perfect partner's strength shown by escorting someone out in a luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Rs removed are not side by side in MR RIGHT, but they come out in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Strength or force is what might means as a noun, as in 'with all his might'.

clue.text: Protester putting rubbish on register

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed next to, the first piece before the second

parts.note: to diss is to rubbish, to disparage
to enter is to register, as in a list

explanation.surface: An activist dumps refuse on the official records.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dissents objects to the established view, which is to protest.

clue.text: Police officer with a boring job going about

indicators.note: going about means turning round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a drag is something tedious

explanation.surface: A constable on a tedious patrol around the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The Garda is the Irish police force; a member is also called a garda.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ireland the word is used for an individual member of the national police.

clue.text: Thursday: we'd met clueing to cause bewilderment with extra complication

indicators.note: an extra complication jumbles the letters into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter admits that their Thursday puzzle was meant to baffle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clueing' is only a link; 'with extra complication' scrambles THURSDAY WE'D MET.
explanation.definitionFit: To muddy something is to make it murky, and figuratively to make a situation confusing.
